ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
Ceasefire in North-East 
† *161. SHRI DRUPAD BORGOHAIN:  Will the Minister of HOME 
AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether any positive results have been brought by unilateral ceasefire 
in Jammu and Kashmir and unconditional ceasefire in Nagaland; 
(b) if so, why such type of unilatera l and unconditional ceasefire is not 
announced in Assam and other affected States of North-Eastern Region to 
bring peace in these States; and 
(c) whether considering all the factors Government would take such 
type of steps in these States soon? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRI CHENNAMANENI VIDYA SAGAR RAO): (a) Yes, Sir, the Unilateral 
Peace initiative in J&K and ceasefire with NSCN(I/ M) backed up by ground 
rules in Nagaland have led to positive results. 
(b) and (c) The Government of India and the Government of Assam have 
declared suspension of operations against Bodo Liberation Tiger. This is backed 
up by agreed ground rules. The Government of Manipur has announced a 
unilateral ceasefire with all militant groups in the Slate, for a period of one month. 
No omnibus policy measures can be drawn up for the entire North-East, 
as the situation differs from State to State. However the situation is kept under 
close watch by the Government of India. 
Effect of Ceasefire on militant operations in J&K 
† *165. SHRI N.K. PREMACHANDRAN: Will the Minister of HOME 
AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government think that the ceasefire has considerably reduced 
the militant operations in Kashmir; 
† Starred Question Nos   161 ami 165 were taken together. 
1 

RAJYASABHA [7th March,2001] 
(b) to what extent Government desire to continue the Kashmir ceasefire 
to achieve peace process; 
(c) whether it is a fact that Pakistan has not even pulled back its forces 
from the Line of Control and is still abating infiltration and keeping militancy 
alive there; and 
(d) whether Govemment propose to evolve any package by exploring the 
advantages of ceasefire for initiating pe rmanent peace in Kashmir, if so, the 
details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE 1NTHE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRI CHENNAMANENIVIDYA SAG AR RAO): (a) to (d) A statement is laid 
on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) There has been a perceptible change in the general atmosphere in the 
State of J&K in terms of overwhelming positive response from the public and 
the mainstream political parties to Prime Minister's Peace Initiative. However, 
except on the border/LoC the extent of  violence has not seen any significant 
decline because militants have been hostile to the Peace Initiative. 
(b) The Govemment has reviewed all aspects of the situation in J&K in 
its totality and has benefited from consultations with all political parties that it 
held on Feb. 21, 2001. It was felt that violence must be ended and peace, which 
has been welcomed by the people of J&K, should be given every chance. The 
Government has accordingly decided to further extend the period till 31 May 
2001. Any further continuation of the peace initiative will depend upon a 
comprehensive assessment of all relevant factors including the ground level 
situation in J&K, which is being periodically reviewed at the highest levels. 
(c) There are reports to the effect that consequent to Pakistan's 
announcement of partial withdrawal of troops during third week of December 
2000, certain reserve formations and some formations undergoing training in 
Pakistan Occupied Kashmir moved to their permanent locations. There are, 
however, no inputs to suggest reduction/withdrawal of troops physically 
deployed on the line of control, and it is regrettable that Pakistan still continues 
to promote, encourage, aid and abet cr oss border terrorism in J&K State and 
has not so far shown any inclination to reign in the terrorist groups. 
2 

[7th March, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
(d) The Government is pursuing a multi pronged strategy to bring peace 
and normalcy in J&K. As part of the strategy Govemment has repeatedly 
indicated its willingness to have talks with any group in the State that abjures 
violence. Simultaneously Govemment is determined that law and order is 
maintained and that any act of violence or terrorism in the State is firmly dealt 
with by the security forces. It is also our hope that Pakistan will act, even now, 
and abjure violence, give up its hostile propaganda against India, stop promoting 
and aiding cross border terrorism, and take the path of peace through bilateral 
talks as enshrined in the Shimia agreement and the Lahore Declaration. 
SHRI DRUPAD BORGOHAIN: Sir, I have not got the complete answer to 
part (b) of my question. In the answer, it is stated that, "The Government of 
India and the Government of Assam have declared suspension of operations 
against Bodo Liberation Tiger." But it is not the only militant group there, the 
ULFA is also there, the NDF (B) is al so there. Sir, Assam and several North-
Eastern States arc burning due to the activities of various insurgent 
organisations like ULFA, NDF(B) etc. 
These insurgent organisations have come up out of frustration created 
because of the sheer negligence shown by the Centre, in one way or the other, 
to the region, in the past. These insurgent organisations consist of Indian 
citizens of the region. 
Sir, in such a situation and considering the positive results of 
unconditional ceasefire with NSCN (IM)  in Nagaland and also considering 
the positive signs of the ceasefire in Jammu and Kashmir, I would like to 
suggest the Ministry of Home Affairs to announce an unconditional ceasefire 
with the ULFA and other militant organisations of the region also, with a view 
to bring them to the negotiating table so that permanent solution to this 
problem could be arrived at. It will also help in preventing the senseless 
fratricidal killings in the region and in  bringing peace to the region. So, I 
would like to know from the hon. Home Minister whether he will consider 
announcing an unconditional ceasefire with the ULFA, the NDF(B) and other 
militant organisations of the region. If so, what is the time frame? If not. what 
are the reasons therefor? 
SHRl CHENNAMANENIVIDYA SAGAR RAO. Sir, so far as the people 
of Nagaland are concerned, they have welcomed the peace process and they 
have also started coming out in the open to demand the continuation of the 
peace process and an end to the violence as well as an end to the factional 
clashes and extortions. So far as the issue of Nagaland is concerned, it has been 
decided to extend the unilateral ceasefire and the results have been very good. 
3 

RAJYASABHA [7th March,2001] 
As far as (he ULFA and other militant organisations, as mentioned by the hon. 
Member, are concerned, it is not being considered because there is no initiative 
from the local people and militant organisations. 
SHRI DRUPAD BORGOHAIN: Sir, my second supplementary is, 
nowadays, in Assam, Indians are killing Indians; Assamese are killing Assamese 
and Bodos are killing Bodos. AH these killings are being condemned by all the 
recognised political parties; by all the social organisations and by all the genuine 
people. Some people say that some of these killings are perpetrated at the 
behest of the ISI, but most of the people in Assam experience another 
phenomenon, i.e., some killings are perpetrated by insurgent and militant 
organisations of the region and some other killings, known as secret killings, 
are perpetrated by a section of police and security forces in collaboration with 
some of the surrendered elements. Sir, to  prevent these killings by militants, 
negotiation is the best means, but killings made by a section of police and 
security forces using some surrendered elements are to be prevented by the 
Home Ministry by adopting a correct policy. So, Sir, I would like to know from 
the hon. Home Minister whether he is aware of all these phenomena which are 
prevailing in Assam. If he is aware of it,  what action he is taking; and if not, 
whether he will study or re-study the situation thoroughly and do the needful? 
This is my second supplementary. 
SHRI CHENNAMANENIVIDYA SAGAR RAO:The Government is ready 
to talk to any militant groups that eschew violence and come to the mainstream. 
So far as the allegation that some'people are being killed by the security forces 
is concerned, I would tike to say that there is no truth in it. It is denied. 
SHRI NX. PREMACHANDRAN: Sir, thank you, Mr. Chairman, for 
clubbing these two questions. Regarding the unilateral ceasefire, the statement 
which has been given by the hon. Minister specifically states that, except on the 
border, the LoC, the extent of violence has not seen any significant decline, 
because militants have been hostile to the peace initiatives. Sir, it is a welcome 
step which has been taken by the Government in declaring the ceasefire during 
the holy Ramzan period, and that has been extended for a further period of three 
months. I would like to know from the hon. Minister what initiative has been 
taken by the Govemment to bring peace in the Valley, because it is an admitted 
fact that even after the ceasefire, killings of innocent people are going on. Does 
the Government have any policy to br ing peace in the Valley or whether any 
talk have taken place in this regard/ What initiative did the Govemment take to 
bring peace, because mere declaration of  ceasefire will not give any result? I 
would like to state that if the Govemment has any policy to bring peace and if the 
4 

[7th March,2001] RAJYASABHA 
ceasefire will not give any result? I would like to state that if the Government has 
any policy to bring peace, and if the ceasefire has to be fruitful, then, something 
has to be given and something has to be brought into. What policy is being 
pursued by the Government so as to initiate talks with Pakistan so that the ceasefire 
becomes meaningful? I would like to ask from the hon. Minister all these things. 
SHRI CHENNAMANENI VIDYA SAGAR RAO: Mr. Chairman, Sir, 
having noted the longings of the people of the Jammu and Kashmir, I would 
like to say that they want restoratio n of peace and normalcy in Jammu and 
Kashmir. Therefore, Sir, this peace mission has been launched by the 
Govemment of India. The hon. Prime Mini ster has also given a statement to 
that effect. The non-initiation of combat operations have been welcomed by 
the local people. Sir, this initiative has been taken to hold talks with all the 
militant groups if they come forward and respond to the non-initiation of 
combat operations that is initiated by the Government. So far as the local 
people are concerned, I would like to say that they are overwhelmingly 
supporting this mission, and for the first time, Sir, the Ramzan festival went on 
peacefully which was never seen in last several years. The Panchayat elections 
were also conducted peacefully. So, over all, there has been an overwhelming 
welcome response from the local people. But, however, these militant groups 
have not yet come forward to negotiate with the Govemment of India in response 
to its offer of talks. 
THE LEADER OF OPPOSITION (DR. MANMOHAN SINGH) : Mr. 
Chairman, Sir, with regard to the peace initiatives that have been taken in the 
North-East, the general perception is th at unless we involve all the affected 
parties, we are going to get only limited results. The Govemment of Nagaland, 
for example, has been feeling that there are other groups, other factions of the 
NSCN who ought to be involved. Will the Govemment inform the House as to 
what is their thinking with regard to involving these other factions of the 
NSCN in the peace process? The second issue, Mr. Chairman, Sir, I would like 
to raise is with regard to the Jammu & Kashmir. All political parties at a meeting 
that was convened by the Prime Minist er had welcomed the peace initiative. 
But it was also, I think, universally agreed that the ceasefire is not an end in 
itself, but it is only a part of the process contributing to the settlement of the 
underlying problem; and expectations have been aroused. The Prime Minister 
in his musings from Kerala had talked of unconventional and imaginative new 
approaches to solve this problem. Would the hon. Home Minister tell us what is 
the thinking of the Govemm ent so that the peace process can be carried over 
from the ceasefire to meaningful negotiations with all affected parties. 
5 

RAJYA SABHA [7th March, 2001] 
THE MINISTER OF HOMEAFFA1RS (SHRI L.K. ADVAN1): Sir, the Leader 
of the Opposition has made two points. One is in respect of involving other 
groups in Nagaland apart from the NSCN(I- M) and the second is in respect of 
Jammu and Kashmir, where there is a need to go beyond merely ceasefire and 
move towards some peaceful settlement. I agree with both die issues. In respect 
of the first issue, I may mention that I had only last week-end visited Nagaland 
and had elaborate discussions not only with the State Government and the 
State officials, but even with various other groups. The Government of India is 
in agreement with the State Governme nt's views that the NSCN(K) and the 
Federal Party also should be involved. These are other militant groups in the 
State along with the NSCN (I-M). And there should be ceasefire also. Informal 
talks have been held and I hope that the Government would be in a position to 
announce some approach in that regard and involve these groups also. 
So far as Jammu and Kashmir is concerned, I may mention that the Ramzan 
peace initiative was addressed to three sections. Firstly, principally the people 
of Jammu and Kashmir. Their response has been very good. Secondly, the 
international community. Their response has been equally good. But the third 
section, which was addressed, was the various militant groups, who, at the 
initiation of Pakistan, have been indulging in cross-border terrorism. There, the 
response has not been satisfactory. Pakistan's own response has been to stop 
shelling on the border, which is welcome,  but is an inadequate response. But, 
we hope that the climate created within  the State, in the people of Jammu and 
Kashmir, and the climate created thr oughout the world against cross-border 
terrorism will act as a kind of a pincer, which would pressurise even Pakistan. 
We hope that Pakistan will exert to rein in these militant groups, who have not 
responded or who have opposed the peace initiative by the Government of 
India. 
Meanwhile we are also determined to see that we start discussions with 
the groups within the Jammu and Kashmir State in respect of what solution 
should be found out. We propose to move in that direction. 
SHRJ W. ANGOU SINGH: Sir, during the ceasefire, the militant outfits of 
the North-East are continuing extortion of money and creating disturbances at 
the National Highways by acts such as burning of trucks, carriage vehicles etc. 
I would like to know whether there is any agreement to cease such occurrences 
on the National Highways Nos. 39 and 53 so that such disturbances may not 
happen in future. 
6 

[7th March, 2001 ] RAJYA SABHA 
SHRI L.K. ADVANI: I would admit that in respect of ceasefire, instances 
of extortions or arson of this kind have been happening and these are violations 
of the ground rules. It has been the effort of the Security Forces to see that the 
ground rules are observed. Even in our discussions with the various militant 
groups, this point is emphasised again and again. It is true that during the 
period of last three years of ceasefire killings and murders have come down, but 
the other violations of the ground rules are there. 1 would not deny it. It is our 
consistent endeavour to see that these are curtailed. 
DR, ARUN KUMAR SARMA: Mr. Chairman, Sir, whatever may be the 
intention of the Government to bring peace to the North-Eastern Region, 
through the ceasefire process, we welcome that. So far, the ceasefire could not 
bring any peace to the region because of the inadequate directions and the 
ground rules. For example, during the period of late Shri Jayaprakash Narayanji, 
when there was a ceasefire, there was a total surrender of arms by the militants. 
The militants were not allowed to operate according to their own whims. Now, 
what is happening in the North-East is, after the ceasefire, the extremists are still 
holding the ground. They are indulging in extortions and killings not only in 
one part, but in other parts of the region. The NSCN is not confined to only 
Nagaland. Now, they have crossed over  to Arunachal Pradesh. They have 
crossed over to Manipur and Assam. They are indulging in extortions and 
killings. Therefore, there is some inadequacy in the ground rules. 
Number two is, regarding surrendered militants. The surrender of the 
militants has started long back. Till now, more than 2,000 militants have 
surrendered, but their rehabilitation is very much inadequate. Many of these 
surrendered militants continue to extort money in order to eke out their livelihood. 
So, I want to know whether the Government has any positive and effective 
steps to deal with the ceasefire; and also to rehabilitate the surrendered militants 
so that the actual peace process can be initiated. I want to know from the Home 
Minister whether any progress has been made in the talks with the militants 
because in his reply the indication about the talks is very insignificant. 
SHRI CHENNAMANENIVIDYA SAG AR RAO: Mr. Chairman, Sir, so far 
as the ground rules are concerned, they were valid up to 31 -7-2000. In January, 
2000 they were revised. According to the ground rules for the ceasefire, that 
were finalised between the Government of India ard the NSCN on the 30th 
January, 2001. there would be no offensive operations like ambush, raids, attacks 
leading to death, injury, damage or lo sses to the property. All precautions are 
being taken. Patrolling by the Indian Army and the para-military forces to check 
7 

RAJYASABHA [7th March,2001] 
the extortions, their movements, protection of convoys and to prevent offensive 
operations like ambush, raids and attacks leading to death, injury and damage 
have been taken. Pursuant to the ground rules, extortions have been prevented. 
So far as the surrendered militants are concerned, they are being looked 
after separately. They are fed in the camps. A monthly amount is being paid to 
them for their rehabilitation. All necessary steps are being taken to bring them 
into the mainstream. 
SHRI SHANKAR ROY CHOWDHURY: Mr. Chairman, Sir, the hon. Home 
Minister just now mentioned that th e unilateral ceasefire announced by our 
Prime Minister has produced an excellent  effect on the people of Jammu and 
Kashmir as well as on the international community. But the people to whom this 
ceasefire offer has been made have not re sponded which is very obvious. But, 
according to the Press reports, our un ilateral ceasefire which was a blanket 
ceasefire, even if the oppon ent had not accepted, it has really resulted in the 
movement of the militants in Jammu and Kashmir entering a new phase of 
violence. That means, since November, since Ramzan, when this ceasefire was 
introduced, militants have taken advantage to regroup themselves. Now we are 
having a series of Fidayeen attacks which were not there earlier. In the latest 
extension of the ceasefire, the Prime Minister has said that we would take action 
against those people who would violate the ceasefire. But the impression we 
get from the media is there are still restrictions on the security forces in taking 
offensive operations. So, my question is, are there any restrictions on the 
armed forces in Jammu and Kashmir in taking offensive operations to search 
and destroy the militants? 
SHRI L.K. ADVANI: Mr. Chairman, si r, the hon. Member is naturally 
concerned about how the security forces would be viewing these matters. 
Firstly, I would like to emphasise that in taking these decisions of the Govemment 
and the peace initiative announced by the Prime Minister, the security forces 
had been fully a party. Secondly, it is a mistaken notion that these peace 
initiatives mean abandonment of our Fight against militancy. It is not. Even 
during this period of "ceasefire"—we had never used the formal word 
"ceasefire"—as many as 227 militants have  been killed by the security forces, 
in the last three and a half to four months . It is true that these days, there is a 
concentration of "fidayeen" attacks. "Fidayeen", these suicide squads, are 
mainly comprised of mercenaries, not people from Kashmir, not people from this 
country. And they had been worked up with a kind of fundamentalist passion 
because of which "fidayeen' attacks do take place. They had been taking place 
8 

[7th March, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
earlier also. But these attacks do get a lot of publicity and create an impress: on 
as if our battle against the militants has been somewhat abandoned, which is 
not so. The security forces have been instructed not even to wait for the other 
party to attack, but if they find people moving about with arms, they are free to 
take initiatives and see that the militants are suppressed. 
SHRI NTLOTPAL BASU: Sir, notwithstanding the claims by the Govemment 
that the situation is generally improving and a lot of initiatives have been taken 
in the North-East, we are actually witnessing that new areas and new 
organisations are being drawn into the vortex of mindless militancy. The latest 
example is the heinous attack on the GNLF supremo, Subash Geising in the 
Darjeeling hills. Press reports also suggest the involvement of the Gorkha 
Liberation Organisation, and in the actual operation, the NSCN-Kaplong group 
might have been involved. This also takes place in the background of press 
reports which say that the IS1 headquarters for the region has been shifted from 
Bangkok to Nepal. And some of these elements have been actually apprehended 
from Nepal. So, what comprehensive plan does the Govemment have for the 
region because notwithstanding the claims of the Govemment, actually, there 
is a ground-swell of new militant activities extending to new areas? 
SHRI L.K. ADVANI: The Government of India shares the concern of the 
West Bengal Government and the hon. Member's concern about this attack on 
Subash Geising and the possibility of other militant organisations, apart from 
the dissidents within his own camp, having engineered this. It cannot be ruled 
out. It is true, Our approach, in respect  of the areas surrounding, where the;, 
take refuge, or which they try to convert into bases, is to see that the Nepalese 
Government, the Bhutanese Government, the Myanmar Government, the 
Bangladesh Government, work hand-in-hand with us in suppressing these 
elements. And I must say that all thes e Governments have been cooperating 
though in their own way and to their limited extent. In fact, this is one reason 
why it is not possible for the Govemment to agree with the proposal being 
made by certain elements that we should unilaterally declare ceasefire in respect 
of the North-East militant organisations because we would like to see that all 
these various countries, Bhutan, Nepal, Bangladesh and Myanmar, do cooperate 
with us fully in suppressing these elements. 
If a unilateral ceasefire were declared as it is being suggested by some hon. 
Members, it would only make them feel that nothing needs to be done from out side. 
In case of Jammu and Kashmir, it is a different situation, because of which we took a 
peace initiative, even unilaterally, knowing fully well that it would take us long to 
9

pressurize Pakistan into reining in these organisations. So far as the apprehensions of 
the Hon. Members are concerned, I can only say that the Govemment of India shares 
them and is conscious that we need to take effective action.

Accidental explosion of anti-tank missile 
    *163.  SHRI C.M. IBRAHIM:  
               DRY. LAKSHMI PRASAD: 
Will the Minister of DEFENCE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether a short range anti-tank missile on display in the highly 
sensitive zone of the Bharat Dynamics Ltd. went-off accidentally during an 
inspection visit of the Defence Secretary and exploded killing the Quality 
Control Supervisor and injuring several others; 
(b) if so, the reasons for exhibiting a live missile instead of a dummy 
missile; 
(c) the result of the inquiry into the accident; and 
(d) the action taken against the official responsible for the mishap? 
THE MINISTER OF DEFENCE (SHRI GEORGE FERNANDES): (a) to (d) 
On 4th January, 2001 during the explanation of the working and loading of a 
launcher at Bharat Dynamics Limited, Hyderabad, the accidental firing of a 
short range anti-tank missile took place. This resulted in outbreak of fire and 
also the death of a Quality Control Inspector, and injury to three other officers. 
The missile did not explode but there was slow combustion of the explosive. 
21 

RAJYA SABHA [7th March, 2001 ] 
A Committee was constituted immediately to investigate the causes of 
the accident; to list out the violations in the security and safety procedures 
which could have led to the accident and to fix responsibility for the lapses and 
also to suggest remedial measures to avoid such accidents. The Committee has 
since submitted its report. The Committee has concluded that the accident was 
not as a result of any sabotage but because of human error in wrongly loading 
a missile and pressing the push button (triggering) on the launcher in the 
process of explaining its working. The Investigation has also concluded that 
the presence of the launcher in the building used for assembling the missiles 
was a contributory factor. 
Major penalty proceedings against four officers of BDL have been ordered. 
The explanation of the CMD, BDL, on the various lapses has also been called for.

Losses in power sector 
† * 167. SHRI JANESHWAR MISHRA: Will the Minister of POWER 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that 40 per cent of the total electricity produced in 
the country is wasted in the form of transmission and distribution and out of 
the remaining 60 per cent, 20 per cent electricity is stolen; 
(b) if so, whether it is also a fact  that the country suffers a loss of 
Rs. 37,000 crores every year in the power sector; and 
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
23 

RAJYASABHA [7th March, 2001] 
(c) if so, the steps being taken by Govemment to improve the power sector? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRl SURESH PRABHU): (a) to (c) On all 
India basis, metered supply accounts for about 40% of the energy sent out by the 
generating stations. In most States, the supply to the agricultural sector for irrigation 
pump-sets and to households below poverty level are not metered. The loss 
sustained during transmission and transformation stage accounts for about 25%, 
according to the figures reported by the State Power Utilities. The balance 35% 
includes supply to unmetered category and losses due to theft/pilferage. 
Theft of energy has been made a c ognizable offence under the Indian 
Electricity Act, 1910. Guidelines for Energy Audit and for reduction of 
Transmission & Distribution losses have been issued by the Central Electricity 
Authority. State Governments/State Power Utilities are being provided funds 
by the Power Finance Corporation at concessional rates for installation of 
meters at all levels. 
In the Chief Ministers' / Power Ministers' Conference held on 3.3.2001 
it was resolved that State Governments/State Power Utilities would take the 
following steps to reduce technical and commercial losses:— 
(i)    Energy audit at all J1 KV feeders will be made effective within the 
next 6 months and accountability fixed at the local level. (ii)     An 
effective Management Information System (M.l.S.) for this 
purpose will be made operational. (iii)    On the basis of the above, 
an effective programme will be launched 
for identifying and eliminating power thefts in the next 2 years. 
(iv)    Full metering of all consumers will be completed by December. 
2001. (v)    The quality of power supplied especially in rural areas 
will be 
improved through the APDP. 
Under the Accelerated Power Development Programme (APDP), fifty 
distribution circles have been identified in the first phase for strengthening the 
distribution system. An Expert Committee has been constituted to assist State 
Governments/State Power Utilities in the areas of project formulation, 
implementation and monitoring/evaluation in all the distribution circles. These 
measures will result in achieving a significant reduction of loss at the distribution 
stage and will also help in improving the financial health of State Power 
Utilities.

Strike by coal miners regarding privatisation of the industry 
* 177. SHRI RAMDAS AGARWAL: Will the Minister of COAL be pleased 
to state: 
(a) the policy of Government with regard to the mining and exploration of 
coal as at present; 
(b) whether Government have taken the decision to privatise the coal 
industry; 
(c) if so, whether the workers in various coal mines have been on strike on 
the issue of privatisation of coal mines; and 
(d) what remedial steps Government propose to take in this regard as well 
as to upgrade the coal sector? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OFTHE MINISTRY OF COAL (SHRI SYED 
SHAHNAWAZ HUSSAIN): (a) and (b) Private coal mines were nationalized in 
1972 and 1973. In 1993. private sector participation in coalmining was allowed 
by allowing coal mining for captive use by companies engaged in production of 
iron and steel, power generation and washing of coal obtained from a mine. 
Later on, companies engaged in cement production were also allowed coal 
mining for their captive use. 
39 

RAJYA SABHA [7th March, 200)] 
Recent assessment about the demand and indigenous supply position of 
coal over the next decade shows a gap of  30.06 million tonnes, 162.28 million 
tonnes and 260.30 million tonnes dur ing 2001-02, 2006-07 and 2011-12 
respectively. Public sector alone will not be able to mobilize adequate resources 
to step up coal production to meet the ever increasing demand. The Central 
Government have, therefore, decided to allow Indian companies to do coal 
mining without the restriction of captive consumption and to engage in 
exploration of coal, subject to appropriate legislative changes. 
(c) Some trade union organisations have been opposing the opening up 
of various areas of the national economy, including coal, to the private sector. 
The All India Worker's Federation, a trade union organisation affiliated to CITU, 
went on strike from 20th November, 2000 to 22nd November, 2000 in support of 
a number of demands which included opposition to the private sector's entry in 
coal mining. 
(d) The Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Amendment Bill, 2000 has been 
introduced in the Rajya Sabha, which seeks to allow Indian companies to 
undertake non-captive coal mining in th e new blocks of coal and lignite and 
also exploration of coal and lignite re sources. The steps taken to upgrade the 
coal sector include measures for improvement in productivity, capacity utilisation, 
quality enhancement and consumer satisfaction.

Load shedding in the Northern Grid  
* 179. SHRl B J. PANDA: Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is fact that there have been massive load shedding in the 
Northern Grid; 
(b) whether power breakdown is frequently taking place in the Northern 
States; 
(c) if so, the reasons therefor; and 
(d) the steps taken to improve the power situation in Delhi and also in 
other Northern States? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SURESH PRABHU): (a) Northern 
Region suffers from power shortage both in terms of peak demand (MW) and 
energy (MU). During the period April, 2000-January, 2001, Northern Region 
as a whole experienced energy and peak shortages of 6.7% and 8.6%, 
respectively. During the same period, the different States of Northern Region 
experienced energy and peak shortages varying from 1.8% to 14% and 0% to 
16.8%, respectively. In order to maintain the grid frequency within safe limits, 
power cuts/load shedding are resorted to in different States depending upon 
the mismatch between demand and availability on day to day basis. 
(b) during last six years, there were two major grid disturbances in the 
Northern Region on 20.12.1996 and 2.1.2001 leading to the total collapse of the 
Northern Grid covering all States and nine partial grid disturbances affecting 
more than one State. 
(c) According to the Central Electricity Authority, low frequency operation 
of the regional grid due to mismatch in power availability and demand, lack of 
spinning reserve in the system, lack of adequate redundancy in the transmission 
system, low voltage at nodal grid points due to inadequate capacitor installation, 
inadequate relief from the under frequency relays at the pre-set frequency 
levels etc. are the primar y reasons for grid disturbances leading to power 
breakdowns. 
(d) In order to mitigate the power shortage in Northern Region States 
including Delhi, besides firm shares, a llocation is made from the unallocated 
quota of the Central Sector Power Stations in the Northern Region keeping in 
view the relative shortages and emergen t/seasonal requirements. In addition, 
special allocations have also been made to Delhi, J&K, Haryana and Rajasthan 
from unallocated quota of Western Region on temporary basis to take care of 
41 

RAJYASABHA [7th March,2001] 
increased irrigation and seasonal requirements of these States. UP is also being 
provided assistance of about 60 MW from the surplus power of Eastern Region. 
Further, action is being taken pending completion of the line for terminating 400 
KV Biharsharif-Allahabad D/C line at Sarnath sub-station of UPPCL by April, 
2001 which will enhance the export of surplus power from Eastern Region to 
Northern Region from existing 60 MW to 350-500 MW. Other measures such as 
Renovation, Modernisation and Uprating of old and inefficient generating units, 
reduction of T&D losses, installation of shunt capacitors etc. have also been 
taken to improve the power situation in the Northern Region. Capacity addition 
of 11736 MW and 10573 MW has also been programmed in Northern Region in 
Xth and Xlth Plan periods, respectively. In the NCT of Delhi, DVB is executing 
Pragati CCGT (330 MW) project. The expected date of commissioning of 1st 
Unit of this plant in January, 2002,2nd Unit in March, 2002 and complete plant 
by November, 2002. In addition, Delhi will also be entitled for a share of power 
from the new Central Sector Power Stations envisaged during Xth and Xlth 
Plans in the Northern Region.

Mines Rescue Stations  
1155. SHRI JIBON ROY: Will the Minister of COAL be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Mines Rescue Stations were working under a separate 
organization in the past; 
(b) if so, whether they were handed over to Coal India Ltd. by 
Government; 
(c) if the answer to (b) is positive the reasons therefor; 
(d) whether in the rescue organization the work was allotted to workers 
by rotation; 
(e) if so, whether it has affected the rescue organization in coal mines; 
and 
(f) The steps being taken to ensure pr oper rescue operations for coal 
mines? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF COAL (SHRI SYED 
SHAHNAWAZ HUSSAIN): (a) Yes, Sir. In pursuance of the provisions of the 
44 

[7th March, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
Mines Act, 1952 read with the Coal Mines Rescue Rules—1959, as amended 
from time to time, the coal mines rescue stations were being administered 
through the Central Coal Mines Rescue Stations Committee under the Ministry 
of Labour. 
(b) In 1983, the Government of  India, in accordance with the 
recomendations made by the third conference on safety in mines, decided to 
vest the responsibility for the rescue and recovery work on the mines 
management. The Mines Act, 1952 was amended to provide for framing new 
rescue rules and making it obligatory fo r managements to establish, maintain 
and manage rescue stations themselves. This amendment came into effect on 
31 -5-1984. The Ministry of Labour vide Memo No. W-12025 / 7 / 83-M.I. dated 
28-3-85 transferred the rescue station to Ministry of Coal. The Coal Mines 
Rescue Rules, 1959 was replaced by the Mines Rescue Rules, 1985. Which 
came into effect from 1.4.1985. With the coming into effect of the new rescue 
rules, the Central Coal Mines Rescue Stations Committee ceased to exist and 
the rescue stations along with their staff, officers and equipment were transferred 
to the coal companies by the Ministry of Coal. 
(c) With the growth of the coal indust ry the need for expansion of the 
rescue organization with enhanced facility was felt. In the third conference on 
safety in mines held on 15 /16 July, 1975 it was recommended that the companies 
should establish their own rescue stations. The rescue stations needed large 
scale revamping and a large number of new rescue stations and rescue rooms 
were urgently required to be set up. 
(d) Active rescue trained persons (workers) employed at rescue stations 
arc kept in all the three shifts in rotation. 
(e) No, Sir. It has not affected the rescue organization in the mines. When 
any emergent situation arises in the mines rescue trained persons attend the 
rescue and recovery work immediately without delay and continue to attend 
the said work whenever they are called tili rescue and recovery work is 
completed. 
(f) The taken over rescue stations of the erstwhile CCMRSC needed large 
scale revamping and a large number of rescue stations and rescue rooms were 
required to be set up to provide necessary rescue services to the operating 
underground coal mines in compliance of the Mines Rules, 1985. With this 
objective in view CIL constituted an expert committee to suggest a 
comprehensive plan for modernization of the rescue services. Based on the 
recommendations of this committee detailed project reports for modernization 
45 

RAJYA SABHA [7th March, 2001] 
of rescue stations and construction of new ones^were drawn up for 
implementation. Compliance of statutory requirement of having rescue 
stations(RS) / rescue rooms (RR) within 35 km. of each operating U/G mine was 
kept in view while deciding sites of these rescue stations. 
The Government of India constituted a Committee {Dubey Committee) 
which approved the locations of different rescue stations/RRs in different 
.subsidiaries and also recommended the broad type of main rescue equipment 
to be provided in RS / RRs. Subsequently, the Standing Committee on Safety in 
Coal Mines recommended the establishment of rescue stations / rescue rooms 
in such a manner in different subsidiary companies that emergent help from 
these rescue establishments are promptly available within half an hour should 
an emergent situation arise in any underground mine. 
Since then the rescue services have been expanded and modernized by 
and large as on date 6 rescue stations, 14 Rescue-Rooms-With-Refresher -
Training-Facilities and 18 rescue rooms are being maintained by CIL. Modern 
state of the art rescue equipment have been provided and rescue personnel 
trained in their use. Modernised training facilities have been provided for training 
of rescuse personnel under simulated conditions.

Safety conditions in Coal Mines  
1165. SHRI K.M. KHAN: Will the Minister of COAL be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the nationalisation of coal mines was done 
primarily due to rise in accidents; 
(b) if so, what are the details of die steps taken to streamline the safety 
conditions in mines since its nationalisation; and 
(c) whether Government are of the view that the privatisation of mining 
sector may prove panacea to the problems of mines safety? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OFTHE MINISTRY OF COAL (SHRI SYED 
SHAHNAWAZ HUSSAIN): (a) Nationalisation of coal mines in 1972 and 
1973 was done with a view to providing adequate investments in coal mines, 
conserve coal resources, ensuring mines safety, environmental protection and 
decent living standards for the coal labour. 
(b) Coal India Limited (CIL) and its  subsidiary companies have been 
taking the following steps to streamline the safety conditions in mines since 
nationalisation; 
(i) Formation of a Structured Internal Safety Organisation both at the 
apex Coal India Limited level as well as at each of the subsidiary 
company level; 
(ii) Revamping the rescue organisation, after taking over the existing Central 
Coal Mines Rescue Committee by the coal companies, by constructing, 
equipping and staffing new rescue stations and rescue rooms; and 
provision of modem equipments and modem training facilities; 
(iii) Promoting workers' participation in safety management through 
bodies, where workmen's representa tives participate right from the 
mine level safety committees to the apex CIL level, Coal India Safety 
Board and the National Level Standing Committee on Safety in Coal 
mines; 
(iv) Installation of computerised continuous environment monitoring in 
some fiery mines and highly gassy mines; 
57 

RAJYA SABHA [7th March, 2001] 
(v) Examination of each mine before every monsoon to assess the danger 
of inundation from both surface an d underground sources of water 
and preparation of suitable action plans for preventive measures against 
the same; 
(vi) Regular periodic safety audit of mines by experienced mining and 
electrical/mechanical engineer s to undertake and their 
recommendations, implemented; 
(vii) Designing of roof support systems in the development workings in 
underground mines by scientific support systems based on rock-mass-
rating studies; 
(viii)  Progressive use of steel support in underground mines; 
(ix) Greater use of quick-setting cement capsule grouted roof bolts for 
support in development workings in underground mines; 
(x) Reduced exposure of workers to mining hazards by mechanisation of 
loading operations by increasing use of Side Discharge Loaders and 
Load Haul Dumpers in the underground mines; 
(xi) Thrust on training and retraining of workmen, supervisors to increase 
safety awareness of the workmen; 
(xii) Formulation of a comprehensiv e action plan to reduce accidents in 
opencast mines and at surface of mines. 
(c) The Government is aware of the need to undertake adequate 
measures to ensure mines safety when  the private sector enters the coal 
sector. To this end, the Bill, which proposes to amend the Coal Mines 
(Nationalisation) Act, 1973 to allow Indian companies both in public sector 
and private sector to do non- captive coal mining, seeks to confer powers on 
the Central Government to frame suitable rules, which will, inter alia, lay 
down norms for location of coal mines, minimum size of mines and such 
other conditions that may be necessary to ensure mines safety. In addition, the 
extant statutory provisions in regard to mines safety will also govern coal 
mining practices of private sector entrants.

Chinese activities along LAC 
1167. SHRl R PRABHAKAR REDDY: Will the Minister of DEFENCE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn to the statement of 
the Chief of Army Staff reported in the Hindustan Times dated 15th January, 
2001, to the effect that the Chinese activities along the Line of Actual Control 
(LAC) are creating some problem between the two countries; 
(b) if so, Government's reaction thereto; 
(c) whether the position stated by Chief of Army Staff was brought to the 
notice of the Chinese Leader Mr. Li Peng during his visit to India; 
(d) if so, Government's reaction thereto and if not, the reasons therefor; 
and 
(e) whether the matter is to be formally taken up with the Chinese 
Government and if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF DEFENCE (SHRI GEORGE FERNANDES): (a) to 
(e) Government's attention has been drawn to the statement of the Chief of 
Army Staff (CoAS) appearing in The Hindustan Times dated 15.1.2001 under 
the caption "Chinese activities along LAC creating problems". 
The resolution of boundary question between India and China is 
outstanding. The two sides have also differences in the perception of the Line 
of Actual Control (LAC) in the border areas. Pending clarification of the LAC, 
the two sides have been carrying out normal border management activities 
including construction of tracks and patrolling upto their respective perception 
of the LaC. The perceived violations of the LAC are taken up by both sides 
through diplomatic channels and also at the ground level through Border 
Personnel Meetings/Flag Meetings. 
The statement of CoAS referred to hereinabove needs to be viewed in the 
above context. CoAS had referred to certain degree of stabilisation on the LAC, 
even while speaking of the differences in the perception of the two countries 
about the actual alignment of the LAC. 
India and China have been discussing the boundary question in the 
framework of the India China Joint Working Group and the India China Expert 
Group of diplomatic and military officials. Both sides have reiterated the objective 
of seeking a fair, reasonable and mutually acceptable settlement of the boundary

question through dialogue. The boundary question was discussed in broad 
terms during the recent visit to India of Mr. Li Peng. 
During the recent visit of Mr. Li Peng, Chairman pf the National Peoples

boundary question with him in broad terms. Both sides expressed satisfaction 
at the progress made on LAC clarification exercise.

1249.     SHRIMATI VANG AGEETHA: 
SHRI SOLIPETA RAMACHANDRA REDDY: 
DR. MANMOHAN SINGH:  
SHRl KRISHNA KUMAR BIRLA:  
SHRI P. PRABHAKAR REDDY:  
SHRI P. K. MAHESHWARI: 
Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Enquiry Committee has been appointed to find out the 
reasons for collapse of the Northern Gird; 
(b) if so, the reasons for the collapse of the grid; 
(c) the suggestions made by the Committee to avoid such collapses in 
future; 
(d) whether a similar Committee was also appointed for collapse of a grid 
sometime back and what suggestions were made by that Committee for avoiding 
such collapse in future; and 
(e) the steps being taken by Government to avoid similar collapse in other 
grids in the country? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER (SHRIMATI 
JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) to (c) A major gird disturbance resulted in the 
collapse of the Northern Regional Grid on 2nd January, 2001. An inquiry was 
ordered by the Government on 3rd January, 2001. The Chairman, Central 
Electricity Authority conducted the inquiry and submitted his report on 10th 
January, 2001. Several factors contributed to the grid collapse. One Pole of 
Rihand-Dadri HVDC line was out of service from 14th December, 2000 due to 
multiple failure of converter transformers. This had restricted the transmission 
capability between the eastern part, where all pit-head generation is located and 
western part of the Northern Region, where major load centres are located. On the 
night of I st / 2nd January, 2001, a number of 220 K V and 400 KV lines of the U.P 
transmission system had tripped and th is imposed a severe strain on the 
transmission system. The transmission capability which had been impaired due to 
reduced capability of the Rihand-Dadri HVDC line got further eroded due to 
tripping of major high voltage transmission lines in UP system and this triggered 
grid separation and collapse. The main recommendations of the 
122 

[7th March, 2001 ] RAJYA SABHA 
Commitee to avoid recurrence of such grid collapse are at Statement-I (see 
below). 
(d) A Committee under the Chairmanship of Member (Grid & Operation), 
CEA was appointed to examine the causes leading to grid disturbance on 
20.12.1996 and to suggest remedial m easures. The remedial measures which 
were suggested by the Committee are given in Statement II (See below). 
(e) Regional Load Despatch Centres (RLDCs) have been established in 
each of the five regions to supervise, control and take appropriate measures 
with a view to operate the regional grids in accordance with Indian Electricity 
Grid Code evolved by Central Electricity Regulatory Commission for ensuring 
safety and security of the grid. Minister  of Power has addressed a letter to all 
the Chief Ministers advising them to ensure grid discipline by restricting their 
drawals from the grid in accordance with their allocated quota and grid 
requirement. The important preventive measures being taken to avoid incidents 
of grid failure in future are as follows: 
 
1. Periodic preventive and regular maintenance of all HVDC, 400 KV and 20 
KV lines and sub- stations. 
2. Introduction of free governor mode of operation at all generating stations. 
3. Ensuring proper operation of under frequency load shedding relays in 
SEBs distribution systems. 
4. Implementaion of a rational commercial mechanism which would induce 
SEBs to regulate their drawal and the generators to generate power 
according to schedules, to enable stabilization of voltage and frequency. 
5. Installation of capacitors at load centres of State Electricity Boards. 
Statement-I 
Recommendations of the Committee which conducted the Enquiry in 
respect of Grid Failure on 2.1.2001 
(i)      A time-bound Action Plan may be prepare for properly tuning the 
governors of BBMB to cater to Black Start conditions. 
(ii)      The action to be taken for reactive support for charging 400K V 
Panipat-Dadri line may be finalised. 
(iii)    400K V circuit breakers at Panipat may be replaced with SF6 Circuit 
Breakers.

(vi) A time-bound programme may be prepared for providing Event

(vii) Immediate action may be taken to review the protection scheme for 
400 K.V Unnao-Agra line. Also periodic preventive and regular 
maintenance of its 400 and 220 KV sub-stations and lines, including

(ix) An Action Plan for installing RealTime Voice Recording Facility at all

(x) Simulator training may be arranged on load despatching to all engineers

(xi) The feasibility of introducing "Expert Systems" for contingency

Power Crisis in Northern Region 
1256. SHRl SATISH PRADHAN: Will the Minister of POWER be pleased 
to state: 
(a) the Government's views and reaction to the massive power crisis in 
Northern region on 2nd January, 2001 inflicting a loss of Rs. 300 to Rs. 500 crore 
in industrial production, according to apex industry association; and 
(b) the details of concrete steps taken or proposed to be taken to stabilize 
the transmission and distribution of power in the country? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER (SHRIMATI 
JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) A major grid disturbance resulted in the collapse of 
the Northern Regional Grid on 2nd January, 2001. An inquiry was ordered by 
the Govemment on 3rd January, 2001 The Chairman, Central Electricity Authority 
conducted the inquiry and submitted his report on 10th January, 2001. Several 
factors contributed to the grid collapse. One role of Rihand-Dadri HVDC line was 
out of service from 14th December, 2000 due to multiple failure of converter 
transformers. This had restricted the transmission capability between die eastern 
part, where all pit-head generation is located and western part of the Northern 
Region, where major load centres are located. On the night of 1 st/2nd January, 2001, 
a number of 220 KV and 400 KV lines of the UP. transmission system had tripped 
and this imposed a severe strain on the transmission system. The transmission 
capability which had been impaired due to reduced capability of the Rihand-Dadri 
HVDC line got further eroded due to tripping of major high voltage transmission 
lines in UP system and this triggered grid separation and collapse. 
Immediately after the grid collapse, Minister of Power addressed a letter 
to the Chief Minister of UP and to a ll the Chief Ministers advising them to 
ensure grid discipline by restricting their drawals from the grid in accordance 
with their allocated quota and grid requirements. Secretary (Power) on 11.1.2001 
directed Chairman, Central Electricity Authority to monitor the action taken on 
weekly basis for implementing the recommendations made for preventing 
recurrence of such incidents. The implementation of the Action Plan formulated 
in accordance with the recommendations made by Chairman, Central Electricity 
Authority is being vigorously monitored by Central Electricity Authority and 
Ministry of Power. 
(b) The important preventive measures being taken to avoid such 
incidents in future are as follows: 
1.  Periodic preventive and regular maintenance of all HVDC, 400 KV 
138 

[7th March,2001] RAJYASABHA 
and 220 KV lines and sub-stations. 
2. Introduction of free governor mode of operation at all generating 
stations. 
3. Ensuring proper operation of under frequency load shedding relays 
in SEBs distribution systems. 
4. Implementation of a rational commercial mechanism which would 
induce SEBs to regulate their drawal and the generators to generate 
power according to schedules, to enable stabilization of voltage and 
frequency. 
5. Installation of capacitors at load centres of State ELectricity Boards.

the State Sector would be obtained through internal resources of SEB/utilities,

Shortage of power 
1265. PROF. M.M. AGARWAL: Will the Minister of POWER he pleased 
to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that there is an acute shortage of power in different 
parts of the country; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor; 
(c) what strategy is being adopted by Government to generate sufficient 
electricity in the country; and 
(d) the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER 
(SHRIMATI JAYAWANTIMEHTA): (a) During the period April 2000—January 
2001, the energy requirement in the country was 421273 million units against 
which the availability was 389188 million units, which represents a shortage 
of 7.6%, The state-wise power supply position during April 2000—January 
2001 is given in the Statement. (See below) 
149 

RAJYA SABHA [7th March, 2001 ] 
(b) The main reasons for shortage of power in the country are as follows:— 
(i) Growth in demand for power outpacing the growth in generation. 
(ii) Low frequency conditions in the grid due to inadequate installation 
of shunt capacitors. 
(iii) Shortage of peaking power in the grid. 
(iv) Constraints in transmission, sub-transmission and distribution system. 
(v) Low Plant Load Factor (PLF) of some of the thermal generating units. 
(vi) Low water level in reservoirs affecting hydel generation. 
(c) and (d) The following steps are being taken to improve the generation 
and availability of power in the country: 
(i) Renovation and Modernisation (R&M) and life extension of existing 
old and inefficient generating units. Special fund under the 
Accelerated Power Development Programme for undertaking R&M 
schemes is being provided to States. 
(ii) Speedy implementation of Reforms & Restructuring in the Power 
Sector. 
(iii) Early stabilization of newly commissioned units and overall increase 
in Plant Load Factor of thermal units. 
(iv) Reduction in Transmission and Distribution losses. 
(v) Promoting energy efficiency and conservation measures. 
(vi) Disbursement of loans by the Power Finance Corporation for 
improving operation and maintenance of thermal power stations 
under the Accelerated Generation Programme. 
(vii) Expeditious implementation of capacity addition programme to enable 
doubling of the existing generation capacity by 2012. 
(viii) Maximizing the inter-state and in ter- regional power transfer by 
construction of required transmission links and finally leading to 
formation of the National Grid. 
(ix) formulation of hydel policy for exploitation of hydro potential in the 
country at a faster pace. 
(x) Encouraging and facilitating independent power producers (IPPs) to 
set up their power plants in the private sector.

† 1267. SHRI JANESHWAR MISHRA: Will the Minister of POWER 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that India would suffer a loss of Rupees four lakh 
crores during next twenty years, as a result of the changes brought about by 
Government in Enron Agreement; 
(b) if so, whether it is also a fact that the rate of its 2,000 mega watt 
electricity would be Rs. 8,000 crore; 
(c) if so, who is going to buy such expensive electricity; and  
† Original notice of the Question was received in Hindi 
156 

[7th March,2001] RAJYASABHA 
(d) whether Indian buyers will not be  affected by this agreement of 
Government? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER (SHRIMATI 
JAYAWANTIMEHTA): (a) to (d) As informed by the Govemment of Maharashtra 
(GOM), the total cost of the 2184 MW Dabhol power project being implemented 
by Dabhol Power Company (DPC) (a company promoted by Enron), is around 
US $ 2501.2 million. Phase-1 of the project with a capacity of 740 MW has been 
commissioned since 13th May, 1999 and has been supplying power to the 
Maharashtra State Electricity Board (MSEB), with whom DPC has signed a 
Power Purchase Agreement (PPA). The State Government has indicated that in 
view of the high tariff of power supplied by DPC to the MSEB, it has become 
exceedingly difficult to absorb the power produced by DPC from its Phase-1 
project. According to the State Govemment, the monthly collection of MSEB at 
the moment is to the tune of Rs. 850 crores and their expenditure, even without 
purchase of DPC power, is Rs. 950 crores. Therefore, it is beyond the financial 
capacity of MSEB to take the liability of Phase-II of the DPC project. 
GOM, vide their resolution dated 9.2.2001, have constituted an Energy 
Review Committee under the Chairmanship of Dr. Madhav Godbole, Ex-Home 
Secretary, Govemment of India (Gol). The terms of reference of the Committee 
areas follows:— 
(i) To review the position of overall demand and supply of electric power 
in the State, with special reference to the supply of power by projects 
of independent power producers and purchase thereof by the MSEB 
for which Power Purchase Agreements (PPA) have either been signed 
or are proposed.

Power Failure at Panki Power Sub-Station in Kanpur 
1275. SHRI S. RAMACHANDRAN PILLAI: Will the Minister of POWER 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Panki, a small power sub-station on the outskirts of Kanpur, 
which serves as a junction to route power to surrounding up linking stations, 
among Muradnagar and Obra developed a big problem; 
(b) whether it took just two minutes from the time the snag developed at 
Panki for a blackout at these two stations and within two hours six northern 
States saw their lights go out; 
(c) if so, what were the causes of such a big power failure; and 
(d) what safeguards have been taken so that such an incident does not 
occur in future? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER (SHRIMATI 
JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) to (c) several factors contributed to the grid collapse 
on 2nd January, 2001. One pole of Rihand-Dadri HVDC line was out of service 
from 14th December, 2000 due to multiple failure of converter transformers. This 
had restricted the transmission capability between the eastern part, where all 
pit-head generation is located and western part of the Northern Region, where 
major load centres are located. On the night of 1 st/2nd January, 2001, a number 
of 220 KV and 400 KV lines of the U.P. transmission system (including 400 KV 
Obra-Panki line and 400 KV Panki-Muradnagar line) had tripped and this 
164 

[7th March, 2001 ] RAJYA SA BHA 
imposed a severe strain on the transmission system. The transmission capability 
which had been impaired due to reduced capability of the Rihand-Dadri HVDC 
line got further eroded due to triping of major high voltage tmsmission lines 
in UP system and this triggered grid separation and collapse. 
Immediately after the grid collapse, Minister of Power addressed a letter 
to the Chief Minister of UP and to all the Chief Ministers advising them to 
ensure grid discipline by restricting their drawals from the grid in accordance 
with their allocated quota and grid requirements. Secretary (Power) on 11.1.2001 
directed Chairman, Central Electricity Authority to monitor the action taken on 
weekly basis for implementing the recommendations made for preventing 
recurrence of such incidents. The implementation of the Action Plan formulated 
in accordance with th e recommendations made by Chairman, Central 
Electricity Authority is being vigorously monitored by Central 
ElectricityAuthority and Ministry of Power. 
(d) The important preventive measures being taken to avoid such 
incidents in future are as follows:— 
1. Periodic preventive and regular ma intenance of all HVDC, 400 KV 
and 220 KV lines and sub-stations. 
2. Introduction of free governor mode of operation at all generating 
stations. 
3. Ensuring proper operation of under frequency load shedding relays in 
SEBs distribution systems. 
4. Implementation of a rational commercial mechanism which would induce 
SEBs to regulate their drawal and the generators to generate power 
according to schedules, to enable stabilization of voltage and frequency. 
5. Installation of capacitors at load centres of State Electricity Boards.

thefts? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER (SHRIMATI 
JAYAWANTIMEHTA): (a) to (c)The national loss due to theft of power is not

Central Electricity Authority have reiterated its Guidelines for the

Though power distribution falls within the purview of the State 
Governments and the activities pertaining to prevention of theft of electricity 
and removing illegal connection have to be taken care of by the power utilities 
operating under their jurisdiction. Theft of energy has been made a cognizable 
offence under Indian Electricity Act, 1910, and the utilities have to effectively 
implement the provisions of the law to curb theft of electricity. 
Some of the steps being taken by various utilities to prevent the theft of 
energy are as under: 
(i) Mass checking drive is carried out periodically by vigilance squads as 
well as field staff. Inspections are being carried out by the District 
wise units of engineers and prosecutions of erring consumers are 
launched by Police Officers manning the anti Power theft Squads. 
(ii)    Installations are being made pilfer proof. 
(iii) A scheme for incentive to info rmants is in vogue. A scheme to 
recognize the performance of individuals, to curb theft of energy by 
providing incentive to deserving officers/employees has been 
introduced. 
(iv) Load inspection studies for major load centres are being conducted in 
routine. 
(v) Penalty for imprisonment is also being imposed on the culprits to 
create moral fear to avoid theft and violation. 
(vi) With the help of computerization of billing process, the abnormal 
consumption of consumers are being detected. If consumption is less 
than 15% of the average energy consumption, cases are immediately 
inspected for detecting tampering of meter/theft of energy. 
In the Power Ministers' Confernece held in February, 2000, the 
following resolutions were made. 
i.      Energy Audit at all levels. 
ii. Time bound programme of 100% metering of all consumers by 
December 2001.

being a State subject, the schemes for supply of safe drinking water to the rural 
habitations of the country are implemented by the State Governments under 
the State sector Minimum Needs Programme (MNP). The Central Government 
supplements the efforts of the States by providing funds under the Accelerated 
Rural Water Supply Programme ((ARWSP). The powers to plan, sanction and 
implement individual rural water supply schemes have been delegated to the

five sectors namely, Primary Education, Primary Health, Rural Shelter, Rural 
Drinking Water and Nutrition. An amount of Rs. 2,500 crore has been provided 
as ACA for these five sectors. A minimum of 15% of the total ACA to each of 
these five sectors has been provided. St ates/UTs are required to decide about 
the remaining 25% of the allocation among the five sectors. A statement 
indicating the funds allocated under PMGY-Rural Drinking Water during the

1285. SHRI SURESH PACHOURI: Will the Mi nister of RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) the magnitude of problem of potable drinking water both in rural as 
well as urban areas; 
(b) how Government propose to solve this problem;

and

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT (DR. (SHRIMATI) RITA VERMA): (a)Asperthe information 
furnished by the State Govemment up to 31.01.2001, out of a total number of 
about 1422664 rural habitations, about 23280 are not covered and about 187139 
rural habitations are partially covered with drinking water supply facilities. 
Further about 2,17,000 rural habitations are reported to be having quality affected 
water sources. It is also reported that, as on 31.3.1997, about 10% of the urban 
population is yet to be provided with access to drinking water supply facilities. 
(b) to (d) Drinking water supply being a State subject, the schemes for 
supply of safe drinking water to the rural habitations of the country are 
implemented by the State Governments. The Central Government supplements 
the efforts of the States by providing funds under the Accelerated Rural Water 
Supply Programme (ARWSP) and Accelerated Urban Water Supply Programme 
(AUWSP). The powers to plan, sanction and implement individual rural water 
supply schemes have been delegated to the State Governments, During the 
first four years of the Ninth Plan period amounts to the tune of approximately

under the ARWSP (till 31-1-2001) and AUWSP respectively. As per the action 
plan prepared by the State Governments, all the rural habitations of the country 
including those of Madhya Pradesh would be provided with access to drinking 
water supply facilities by the year 2004, subject to availability of funds. As far 
as urban areas are concerned, 38 town water supply schemes were targeted to 
be implemented in Madhya Pradesh during the Ninth Plan.

2000. The news item has given a general statement regarding corruption at the 
Panchayat level. No specific observations arc made in the news item regarding 
mis-utilisation of funds. However, the Concurrent Evaluation (June 1993 to 
May 1994) of Jawahar Rojgar Yojana (JRY) revealed that a large portion i.e. 
83.16% of the available funds were spent by the Village Panchayat on 
community development projects at All-India level. The Concurrent Evaluation

on the Employment Assurance Scheme (EAS) revealed that the average utilization 
rate at the district level was as high as 89.9% during 1996-97 and 61.5% at the 
Block level of their notional minimum allocation. 
(b) to (d) The Centrally Sponsored Scheme (CSS) of Rural Development 
being implemented have in-bilt mechanism to prevent mis-utilisation at the 
Implementation level. The mechanism includes submission of Audit Report, 
Utilisation Certificate, non-diversion/non-embezzlement certificate etc. at the 
time of submission of proposals for release of 2nd instalment of the Central 
share. In addition, the Monitoring and Vigilance Committee have been 
constituted at the State, District and Block level to supervise/monitor and oversee 
the implementation of the Rural Development Programmes. Besides, Senior 
Officers of the Ministry of Rural Development also visit pevriodically to review 
the Implementation of the Rural Development Programmes under Area Officer's 
Scheme. The Concurrent Evaluation of different programmes is being 
conducted by the Ministry of Rural Development through independent and 
reputed research institutes/NGO to identif y the problem areas so as to enable 
the Ministry and take corrective action wherever necessary.

Sanitation Programme has been restructured w.e.f 1-4-99. Under the Restructured 
Programme. Total Saintation Campaign is being implemented in a project mode.

during the Ninth Plan period. As such  there are not targets fixed annually.

Safe Drinking Water for Villages in Andhra Pradesh 
1297. SHRl K.M. KHAN: Will the M i n i s t e r  of RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) how many villages/habitations in the State of Andhra Pradesh have 
partially been provided safe drinking water under the Centrally Sponsored 
Scheme; 
(b) what is the number of villages/habitations that are being covered 
during the current financial year 2001- 2002, district-wise; and 
(c) what is the number of villages where safe drinking water is yet to be 
provided, district-wise? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT (DR. (SHRIMATI) RITA VERMA): (a) Rural Water 
Supply being a State subject, schemes for providing drinking water supply 
facilities to rural habitations are implemented by the State Governments with 
the funds provided under the Stat e sector Minimum Needs Programme 
(MNP). The Central Government supp lements the efforts of the State 
Government by providing financial a ssistance under the Accelerated Rural 
Water Supply Programme (ARWSP). Powers have been delegated to the 
States to plan, sanction and implement individual rural drinking water supply 
schemes. 
As per the information received from the Government of Andhra Pradesh 
till 31-1-2001, out of a total number of 69732 rural habitations in the State, 
50315 are fully covered and the remaining 19417 rural habitations are 
partially covered with drinking water supply facilities. 
(b) and (c) About 5400 rural habitations is targeted to be covered with 
drinking water supply facilities by the Government of Andhra Pradesh during 
the current financial year. The covera ge plan for 2001-2002 has not been 
fmalised. As per information furnished by the Government of Andhra 
Pradesh, there is no rural habitation in  the State that does not have access to 
drinking water supply facility. However,  there were 14260 quality affected 
rural habitations in Andhra Pradesh as on 1-4-1999, as reported by the State 
Government. District-wise information is not maintained at the Central level.

1307. SHRI SWARAJ KAUSHAL: Will the Minister of TEXTILES be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether his Ministry had represented to the Finance Ministry against 
the Excise Duty structure on medium scale process houses in the country; and 
(b) what is the impact of the presen t excise and import policies on the 
medium scale process houses in the country in the years 1999-2000 and till 
date? 
217 

RAJYA SABHA [7th March, 2001] 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF TEXTILES (SHRI 
V. DHANANJAYA KUMAR): (a) Yes Sir. 
(b) During the period 1999-2000 and 2000-01, the independent process 
houses including medium scale process houses attracted compounded rate of 
excise duty on stenter/chamber basis.  Under the scheme during the year 
1999-2000, processing units whose average value of processed fabric was 
upto Rs. 30/- sq. mtr., the excise duty payable was Rs. 1.50 lakh per chamber 
per month. In case of average value of processed fabric exceeding Rs. 30/- sq. 
mtr., the excise duty payable was Rs. 2.00 lakh per chamber per month. During 
the year 2000-01 these rates were revised upwards to Rs. 2 lakhs and Rs. 2.5 
lakh per chamber per month respectively. The impact of duty depended on the 
type, quantity and the value of the fabrics processed by the independent medium 
scale process house. In the current budget 2001-02, the stenter/chamber based 
duty has been withdrawn and advalorem rate of duty of 16% [BED 8% + 
AED(ST)] has been imposed with facility for deemed Cenvat credit @ 25% 
and 45% of aggregate duly in respect of cotton fabrics and other fabrics 
respectively The advalorem rate of duty is same as applicable on process houses 
of composite mills. 
As regards impact of import policy, most of the critical processing machinery 
are covered under specified 159 tex tile machinery which were attracting 
concessional rate of basic import duty of 15% during the year 1999-2000 and 
2000-01 as against normal applicable rate of import duty of 25%. In the current 
budget 2001-02, the concessional rate of import duty has been reduced to 5%. 
The grey and processed fabric can be in ported on payment of applicable rate 
of import duty.

Statement 
Major rinding!; of the study on comparative performance of public and 
private sectors in India 
(a) The public sector in India has performed the task assigned to it, 
reasonably well, given the constraints. There are aberrations, but all 
are not of its making. The acquisition and operations of bankrupt 
private sector companies was, fo r example, a result of decision 
imposed on it. 
(b) The public sector's main objective was socially-focussed, in many 
cases by the conception of enterprises and in others by their 
mechanisms. The administered prices  were not commercially viable 
which implied subsidies. Commercial enterprises cannot provide 
large subsidies and generate high profits. 
(c) Empirically, the performance of the pu blic sector, seen in its total 
perspective, is comparable to that of the private sect or, although the 
former's perceived sub-standard performance has received recurrent 
and flashing limelight. On a rationally comparable basis, the 
profitability of CPEs more than matches with that of the total private 
sector. 
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
243 

RAJYA SABHA [7th March, 2001] 
(d) Performance of the public sector in terms of financial parameters has 
been improving markedly since the onset of the economic reforms 
programme. 
(e) It is comparable with the private sector in terms of Economic Value 
added (EVA) and Return on Capital Employed (ROSE). The 
Government has recovered during the last three years more than the 
total capital invested in the form of dividends, interest and taxes. 
(f) Financial failures have frequently occurred in enterprises controlled 
and managed by some of the leading business groups and corporate 
managements applauded for their managements skills, let alone small 
and medium enterprises, the private sector has been facing tough times 
with the onset of economic readjustment programme and the onslaught 
of multinationals. Many have closed down or are sold to MNCs. 
(g) Beyond financial performance, the private sector owner managements 
have been frequent and debilitating defaulters to all stakeholders— 
shareholders, lenders, depositors, vendors, customers and workers. 
(h) Let alone the workers, even the sh areholders have not received a fair 
deal from the private sector with thousands of companies not paying 
dividends defaulting on repayment of deposits and the share prices 
touching incredible lows. 
(i) Large NPAs damaging the ressults of financial institutions and banks 
are indicative of the losses incurred and defaults made by the private 
enterprise entities. So are the large number of sick units. 
(j) The overall dividend record of private corporates has been abysmally 
poor. More than half the number of the listed companies do not pay 
any dividends. Even EPS of privat e sector companies, an indicator 
or profit earning capacity, is low. So is the P/E record—barring a 
small percentage of star performers, 
(k) A large number of sick units in th e public sector are a legacy of the 
private sector. The takenover enterpri ses acquired at the direction of 
the Govemment from time to time and not adequately supported by 
the Government have badly damaged the image of the public sector. 
(1) It is universally admitted that there has been very little autonomy in 
public enterprises. Vital clearan ces for decisions—from conception 
to commissioning to current operations—have often been delayed 
244 

[7th March, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
for months, years and even decades . Many turnaround programmes 
remain non-starters. Apart from the dilatory clearances, there has 
been marked positive interference. 
(m) Despite the bureaucratic procedures with the public sector undertakings 
have had to follow, a high degree of  professionalism has taken place 
with far more focussed and efficient HRD interventions. 
(n) The public sector has established management and training institutes 
of which any industrial or service organisation can be proud. 
(o) The public sector has undertaking  more effective R&D effort at the 
enterprise level. 
(p) PS Us have attended to the welfare and social dimension of the work 
force in particular and the community in general in a much more 
effective manner. 
(q) Since the onset of the last d ecade or so, especially since the 
announcement of the enconomic refo rms programme, public sector 
has come under scathing and undeserved attacks, which have tended 
to destabilise it. 
(r) Underterredby the changing and hi ghly destablishing pronouncements 
including those on privatisation and disinvestment, which have created 
uncertainties and demoralisation, the public sector has produced 
enough evidence that it marches on to meet the challenges of the new 
millenium. 
(s) PSUs after PS Us are working on a new agenda of global competitive-
ness and have envisioned—even launched—expansion, 
diversification, modernisation and restructuring programmes. These 
moves should generate handsome retuns. 
(t) PSUs have also entered and are proposing to enter into strategic 
alliances and joint ventures within the public sector and between the 
public sector, on the one hand, and domestic and foreign enterpises, 
on the other. Some of these plans will expand rather than contract the 
Indian public sector. 
(u) Although continuing to be owned by the government, budgetary 
support, sometimes critical, has been  denied to the public sector 
enterprises. 
245 

RAJYA SABHA [7th March, 2001] 
(v) PSUs are not basing their ambitious plans of expansion, diversification 
and technology upgradation on fiscal s upport. They are confident of 
generating surpluses and of mobilising the resources by accessing the 
market on their own. 
(w) Since the onset of the economi c reforms programme, even the 
Govemment has taken some positive steps declaring selected CPEs 
as navaratna and mini-ratnas with some doses of autonomy. 
(x) The structure, vision, goals and systems of the public sector have gone 
through a whole reformation. Almost  at the threshold of the year 
2001, the public sector in India is no longer the public sector of the 
early 1980s or even the late 1980s. 
(y) Assured of the freedom to operate under new standards of corporate 
governance now advocated by professional dispensation, the public 
sector is confident to be globally competitive. 
(z) Given the dictates of global competition and need for professional 
corporate governance, both sectors are slowly but steadily inching 
towards convergence. Privatisation, as such, is partly a redundant 
and partly an obsolete concept. There is a need to be innovative in 
discovering new models of corporate governance.

1059. SHRI SWARAJ KAUSHAL: Will the Minister of LAW, JUSTICE 
AND COMPANY AFFAIRS be pleased to state:

judicial districts in the Capital on the request of Government;

in the capital?

(SHRI ARUN JAITLEY): (a) to (c) No, Sir.
