Ratio of Judges vis-a-vis pending cases 
† 1066. SHRI RAJNATH SINGH 'SUR YA: Will the Minister of LAW, 
JUSTICE AND COMPANY AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the ratio of number of Judges and pending cases in High 
Courts is much more than the ratio of Supreme Court and District Courts; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor; 
(c) whether there is any concrete plan to dispose of the large number of 
pending cases in the High Courts in the country; and 
(d) if so, the salient features of the same? 
THE MINISTER OF LAW, JUSTICE AND COMPANY AFFAIRS 
(SHRI ARUN JAITLEY): (a) Yes, Sir. 
The approximate ratio of number of Judges and pending cases in High 
Court, Supreme Court and District Courts is 5307,833 and 1661 respectively. 
(b) The problem of pendency of cases in  High Courts is arising due to 
various complex factors. These include  vacant posts of judges, increase in 
the institution of cases on account of aw areness of rights on the part of the 
citizens; enactment of numerous laws creating new rights and obligations, 
industrial development in the country and increased trade and commerce and 
emergence of socio-economic measur es (legislative and administrative), 
touching the life of the citizens at all levels, population explosion, lawyers* 
strike etc. 
(c) and (d) All the High Courts have been requested to follow the steps 
taken by the Supreme Court such as more practical categorisation and grouping 
of cases, to take up for hearing all the cases listed for the particular day as far 
as possible, non-accumulation of defective matters, reservation of more and 
sufficient time slot for old pending cases in chronological order and streamlining 
of administration and manpower of the registry through computer network, 
for bringing down the pendency. The High Courts have favourably responded 
Efforts are being made with the help of the Chief Justice of India and the 
Chief Justices of the High Courts to f ill up all vacant posts of judges in the 
High Courts to expedite disposal of pending cases.

Statement 
Principle, Aims and Objectives of India Habitat Centre 
(i) Develop an integrated physical environment in which various 
professions and institutions dealing with different facts of habitat related 
environmental issues would function, interact and attempt to resolve habitat 
related problems in a co-ordinated manner. 
(ii) Promote awareness in regard to habitat related environmental issues 
including water, air, noise and waste pollution, energy and its conservation, water 
and human waste management and such other matters. 
383 

RAJYA SABHA [7th March, 2001]

cultural and economic context and related to the life style of its people. 
(iv) Inculcate better awareness and sensitivity in regard to all aspects of 
creative productivity including the significance of art in habitat. 
(v) Document all relevant information pertaining to habitat human 
settlements and environmental issues. 
(vi) Advise and if needed, assist the Government in the formation and 
implementation of policies relating to habitat and human settlements. 
(vii) Promote education, research, training and professional development 
on habitat and human settlement and environment related issues. 
(viii) Organise and promote conferences, seminars, lectures, public debates 
and exhibitions in matters relating to habitat, human settlements and 
environment. 
(ix) Offer awards, prices, scholarships and stipends in furtherance of the 
objectives of the Centre. 
(x) Cooperate and collaborate with other national or international 
institutions in furtherance of the objectives of the Centre. 
(xi) Acquire, hold, improve and deve lop lands and construct building and 
related facilities on behalf of the members of the Centre. 
(xii) Organise and maintain residential hostels, restaurants and other 
amenities for its members, their guests and non-members invited by the Centre. 
(xiii) Maintain and keep in good repair alt building and common services. 
(xiv) Constitute or cause to be cons tituted Regional Centres at convenient 
places to promote the objective of the Centre. 
(xv) Do all such other lawful activities as the Centre considers conducive 
to the attainment of all or any of the other objectives.

Demand and Supply of Water in Delhi 
1133. SHRI CO. POULOSE: Will the Minister of URBAN DEVELOPMENT 
AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) the gap between the demand and supply of water in Delhi; 
(b) whether Govemment are aware mat huge gap in demand and supply is 
forcing the people to use ground water resulting in depletion of water level; and 
(c) if so, the steps taken to conserve water? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINI STRY OF URB AN DEVELOPMENT 
AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION (SHRI BANDARU DATTATRAYA): (a) Delhi 
Jal Board has reported that at the present demand for water in Delhi is about 800 
MGD for all uses against which it is able to supply about 630 MGD of water by 
optimization on an average. There is about a gap of 170 MGD of water betwen 
demand and supply. 
394 

[7th March, 2001 ] RAJYA SABHA 
(b) Yes, Sir. 
(c) The following steps have been taken by Delhi Jal Board to conserve 
water :— 
(i) A comprehensive scheme amounting to Rs. 197 lakhs has been approved 
for the work of detection of unaccount ed for water by specialized agencies 
which is under implementation. Latest additional equipments have also been 
procured for detection of hidden leakages. 
(ii) For augmentation in the storage of ground water and control in decline 
of water levels, rain water harvesting projects have been taken up. Work on 
41 such projects has already been completed and 17 are in progress. 
(iii) Govt, of National Capital Territory  of Delhi is creating water storage 
in the reach between Dhansa and Kakr ola regulator in Najafgarh drain to 
raise the ground water level.

1137. SHRI B.J. PANDA: Will the Minister of URBAN DEVELOPMENT 
AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION be pleased to state : 
(a) whether Govemment have identified the major cities in the country 
which are prone to earthquake; 
(b) if so, the details thereof;

(d) if so, the possible preventive and re medial measures adopted in the 
vulnerable zone of Delhi and other metros to face any such eventuality? 
397 

RAJYA SABHA [7th March, 2001] 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION (SHRI BANDARU

which provides mapping of disaster prone areas and the level to which various

(c) Delhi lies in Zone IV Areas falling in Zone V are most prone to

Territory Administrations to make earthquake resistant technology a 
compulsory part of all b u ild in g  regulations. In Delhi, the construction of 
building is governed by the Building Bye-laws which take care of the structural 
safety of the buildings cons true ted/proposed to be constructed. These building 
bye-laws are regulated and implemente d through various agencies like the

strictly curbing any violation of the building bye-laws by any person(s) and

and acts against any unauthorised construction. However, to give a greater 
thrust for making buildings quake resistant and structurally more sound

purporting to amend certain provisions of the building bye-laws which would 
enable greater structural safety of the buildings. 
The Ministry had written to all Chief Secretaries in May 1998 to modify 
their building bye-laws by incorporating earthquake safety measures as per 
specifications formulated by Bureau of Indian Standards. After the earthquake 
in Gujarat, all State Governments have again been requested to take urgent 
action in this regard.

Sewer Crisis Before NCR 
1138. SHRI P. PRABHAKAR REDDY:  Will the Minister of URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the National Capital Region of Delhi is facing a 
major crisis on sewer front resulting in pollution ofYamuna, contamination of 
ground water and mixing of sewage with drinking water supply pipelines; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor; and 
(c) the steps proposed to be taken to  put Delhi sewer system in place 
urgently? 
399 

RAJYA SABHA [7th March, 2001] 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION (SHRI BANDARU 
DATTATRAYA): (a) and (b) Pollution in  river Yamuna in Delhi and the 
National Capital Region is a serious probl em which is mainly due to lack of 
dilution capacity of the river, unauthorised colonies broken trunk and branch sewer 
lines, proliferation of slums on the river bed and mismatch of demand and 
capacity of Sewerage Treatment Plants. The Delhi Jal Board (DJB) have 
informed that in Delhi the present capacity of sewage treatment is 402.4 
MGD which is proposed to be augmented to 512.4 MGD by 2002-2003. 
Presently, waste water generation in Delhi is estimated at 610 MGD of which 
about 32S MGD is being treated. 
The NCR Planning Board have informed that many towns in the NCR 
have sewer system. In Haryana, the colonies being developed by Haryana 
Urban Development Authority (HUDA) and private developers. It is the 
responsibility of respective developers to collect, treat and dispose it off after 
bringing sewage effluent to the desired standards. Area covered under sewerage 
system in the towns varies from 42% - 80% of the total town area. NOIDA has 
been covered 100% by the sewerage system, Ghaziabad 90% Khurja about 
75% and Meerut about 30%. At present one Sewage Treatment Plant (STP) of 
9 mid. capacity is operational in Noida. In Ghaziabad & Meerut Towns, part of 
the sewage is being utilised for irrigation purpose. 
(c) An Action Plan for rehabilitati on of trunk sewers, relocation and 
rehabilitation of slums of river beds, extending the sewage facilities to all areas 
of Delhi, construction of more sewerage treatment plants, trapping of drains at 
their mouth has been prepared by the Govt, of NCT of Delhi which is being 
implemented and monitored through the DJB. This Action Plan has also been 
submitted to the Supreme Court in CWP No. 725/94-AQFM Vs CPCB.

Need to Implement Wheat for Oil agreement with Iraq 
SHRl EDUARDO FLAEIRO (Goa): Mr. Chairman, Sir, the 
Government of India has entered into an agreement with Iraq to sell 
'wheat for oil' and the implementation of the agreement was to begin in 
January last but has not begun so far. The fact is that the agreement 
needs to be approved by the UN Security Council because of 
sanctions against Iraq and the Government of India has not been 
pressing for this approval with a sense of urgency. The agreement is in 
our interest as we are presently burdened with about 27 million tonnes 
of wheat as against the buffer requirement of 19 million tonnes and 
foreign exchange outflow is increasing everyday to pay for oil. 
Government should take immediate steps under article 50 of the UN 
Charter and issue necessary instructions to our Permanent Mission at 
the UN to get the agreement ratified by  the Security Council so that it 
becomes operational without further delay.   Thank you.

DR. M.N. DAS (Orissa): This is regarding Tornado devastation

Need for caution in importing genetically engineered Foods and 
Seeds 
DR. Y. RADHAKRISHNA MURTY (Andhra Pradesh): Sir, my 
Special Mention pertains to the need for caution in importing 
genetically engineered foods and seeds. The Minister for Agriculture 
had sometime back assured the House that the Government of India 
would not allow genetically engineered terminator seeds into the 
country. But we have the disturbing  news that the genetically modified 
foods have found their way into India, as a part of the US aid and relief 
to the flood victims of Orissa. The US is said to have dumped 
unlabelled soyabeans and corns on the rice-eating Orissa population. 
Some senior medical scientists in the AIIMS have alleged that these 
foods have an adverse effect on huma n health. It is worth noting that 
the UK, the EU and several other countries have discouraged import of 
genetically modified foods. Some of them made labelling of these 
foods compulsory. Iceland is said to have totally banned them in their 
feedstock. Some giant companies and retail chains, like Mark & 
Spencers, Sainsbury, Carrefour, Tesco, Unilever, Nestle, Cadbury, Mc. 
Donalds, etc. publicly promised to shun the genetically modified foods. 
The Research Foundation for Science & Technology and Ecology has 
called for a 10-year freeze on 
424 

[7 March, 2001] RAJYA SABHA  
genetic engineering m food and farming, and also for a bio-safety 
mechanism. The International Environmental Group -- Green Peace --
argues that genetically modified foods can damage human health as 
well as the environment. It now frowns at our Government's undue 
hurry to sanction Monsanto trials in India. 
Even the genetically engineered seeds, other than terminator, 
which are entering the country in a big way, can result in development 
of herbicide resistant weeds, named superweeds, which may, in 
course of time, be most harmful to all the crops. It is time that the 
Government of India should tread cautiously in allowing open or 
clandestine entry of genetically modified foods and seeds. 
Let us learn from the caution being shown by the developed 
countries. 
Our Government may well constitute an expert committee of 
bio-scientists, medical luminaries and environmentalists to study the 
problem in depth and advise the Government and the people as to 
future course of action

Diarrhoea Vaccine 
SHRI RAMA MUNI REDDY SIRIGIREDDY {Andhra Pradesh): 
Sir, my Special Mention relates to taking immediate steps for 
launching rotavirus Diarrhoea vaccine. 
Sir, it is very happy to note that  a team of Indo-US scientists 
has developed a new vaccine to check Rotaviral Diarrhoea, which has 
been taking a toll of about 1.5 lakh children, in the age group of 0-5 
years, annually. In our country, children in this age group suffer as 
many as 25 episodes of Rotaviral Diarrhoea as compared to only 5 
episodes in the U.S. It is also shattering to note that one out of five 
infant deaths in India occur due to Rotaviral Diarrhoea. I congratulate 
the Indo-American scientists for th is magnificent achievement which 
will save millions of our children. It is not that there is no vaccine for 
this, but the vaccines, that have been developed by some MNCs in the 
US, Belgium, China, etc., are all useless to 
425 

[7 March, 2001] RAJYA SABHA  
combat viral strains native to India. The problem with this virus is, 
strains native to one country are different from that of the other country 
and, so, universal vaccine is impossible. This joint programme, whiqh 
started in the mid-8Gs, took more than 15 years to find a viral strain, 
from which vaccine can be prepared. This virus affects the children of 
all nations, irrespective of economic development of the country. For 
example, in US alone more than 40,000 children die annually because 
of this. 
I request the hon. Minister of Health to take all possible steps 
on a war-footing so that the vaccine enters into the market 
immediately, at a cheaper rate, so that children gets relief from this 
deadly disease.
